 Can grandparents or relatives contribute to a Trump Account? What to know.
 Rachel Christian · Contributing Writer Tue, October 27, 2026 at 12:22 PM CDT 8 min read If you want to help your grandchild, niece, or nephew build a financial head start, you can contribute to their Trump Account, and you don't need to manage the account to do so. However, there's an annual limit and tax rules. Here's everything you need to know.  
 What is a Trump Account? 
 Created by a 2025 federal tax law, a Trump Account is a special type of traditional IRA for children. Unlike other IRAs, it doesn't require earned income to contribute when the child is a minor. That makes it possible for you to contribute before your grandchild ever lands their first job. 
 Children with Social Security numbers can claim an account if they're under 18 throughout the year the account is established. U.S. citizens born from 2025 through 2028 may also receive a one-time $1,000 federal deposit if an adult elects to claim the money by using Form 4547 . 
 Money goes into low-cost U.S. stock index funds. Earnings grow tax-deferred, though a portion of withdrawals may be taxable.  
 Who can open a Trump Account, and how do grandparents fit in? 
 The Treasury began automatically opening accounts for all eligible children on Oct. 1. However, an authorized adult must still claim and activate the account before relatives can contribute. 
 Parents or legal guardians usually manage the account. Under IRS rules, grandparents can open a Trump Account for their grandchild, but only if a legal guardian, parent, or adult sibling isn't available to do so.  
 You can add money without managing the account. You just need the "authorized adult" (the Treasury Department term for the person who opened the account) to send you a link.   
 How much can grandparents and relatives contribute to Trump Accounts? 
 The IRS contribution limit for Trump Accounts is $5,000 per child in 2026 and 2027. Even if you have multiple grandchildren, each child's account has its own contribution limit. 
 The $1,000 federal payment and qualifying government or nonprofit deposits don't count toward the annual limit.  
 There's nothing you need to do to claim contributions from philanthropic groups or state and local governments. If your grandchild qualifies for one of these programs, the money will be deposited automatically into their Trump Account without a separate application.  
 How to contribute to someone else's Trump Account 
 Contributing to a grandchild's Trump Account is relatively easy. You don't need to enter the child's Social Security number or type in anyone's password.  
 Follow these simple steps to get started: 
 Confirm that the account is active: The Treasury Department auto-enrolled millions of kids, but that doesn't mean someone has claimed and activated the account yet. To do that, a parent or other authorized person must use the Trump Accounts app , verify their identity and relationship to the child, and complete the account activation process. 
 Check the remaining limit: Ask how much other relatives have already contributed before depositing money.  
 Get the contribution link: This will take you directly to the contribution page. The account manager will need to open the child's account, tap the QR code icon beside the child's name, select "Share link," and then send it to you by text or email. 
 Follow the link and fund your gift: Open the QR code link and follow the on-screen instructions. You can add funds electronically by linking your bank account or debit card. Paper checks aren't accepted. Debit card contributions typically get processed right away, while bank transfers can take up to five business days to become available. 
 How to avoid going over the limit when several relatives contribute 
 It's relatively easy to check how much money has already been added to someone's Trump Account.  
 Outside contributors can see how much they're allowed to add when they go to make a deposit. The account manager can also check completed and pending deposits in the app's History section.  
 Fortunately, the platform is designed to prevent overfunding. Once the account hits its $5,000 annual limit, additional contributions are declined, and recurring deposits automatically pause until the next calendar year. 
 If an excess contribution somehow gets through, the account could face a 6% annual tax on the excess amount until it's corrected. 
 For example, if an account is overfunded by $1,000, the account would pay a penalty tax of $60 every year until the excess $1,000 is removed.

 Do contributions to Trump Accounts count as gifts? 
 Putting money into your grandchild's Trump Account counts as a gift in the eyes of the IRS, but that doesn't mean you'll owe taxes on it. 
 In 2026, you can give someone up to $19,000 without triggering gift taxes or having to report those gifts to the IRS in most cases. That limit applies to all the gifts you give that person throughout the year, not just money you put into their Trump Account. 
 For example, say you contribute $3,000 to your granddaughter's Trump Account and give her another $5,000 for her birthday. That's $8,000 in total gifts, well below the $19,000 limit. 
 The $19,000 limit applies to each person individually. So you and your spouse could each give your granddaughter up to $19,000 in 2026 — but keep in mind the Trump Account's $5,000 annual contribution limit still applies. 
 The IRS also introduced special rules in 2026 that let relatives who meet certain requirements contribute to Trump Accounts without filing additional gift tax paperwork. 
 There's a catch, though. If you give more than $19,000 to the same child or have other gift tax reporting obligations, you may need to file a gift tax return. That doesn't automatically mean you'll owe taxes, but it's worth checking with a tax professional if you're making large gifts. 
 Trump Account vs. 529 plan vs. UTMA for grandparents 
 Trump Accounts aren't the only way for relatives to contribute to a family member's investments. Custodial accounts (also known as UTMAs or UGMAs) and 529 college savings plans also let grandparents chip in.

 For college savings, a 529 plan is hard to beat. Some states offer tax breaks for contributions, and qualified withdrawals for education are tax-free and penalty-free.  
 A custodial account gives you more flexibility to invest for your grandchild. Grandparents can open and contribute to these accounts, and there's no annual contribution limit, though gift tax rules still apply. 
 Unlike a Trump Account, which restricts withdrawals until the year the child turns 18, money in a UTMA can be used at any time for expenses that benefit the child, such as a first car or summer camp. 
 The biggest drawback is taxes. Trump Accounts let investments grow tax-deferred. But with a UTMA, dividends, interest, and profits from selling investments can trigger taxes each year.  
 What grandparents should know before they contribute 
 Before gifting, consider these trade-offs: 
 The account isn't for childhood expenses: Ordinary withdrawals aren't allowed until Jan. 1 of the year your grandchild turns 18.  
 You can't take the money back: The money belongs to the child, even if your finances or family relationships change. So make sure to only contribute an amount you're comfortable giving away for good. 
 Control eventually shifts: In the year the child turns 18, traditional IRA rules apply. Your grandchild can keep investing, but withdrawals may trigger taxes or penalties.  
 Investing options are narrow: Funds track broad U.S. stock indexes without built-in bond or international exposure. As with all investing, returns aren't guaranteed.  
 A Roth IRA may be a better option for working teens: If your grandchild earns money from a job, you can help fund a custodial Roth IRA instead. Roth IRAs offer more investment choices and tax-free qualified withdrawals, while money withdrawn from a Trump Account may be subject to income taxes. 
 Bottom line 
 Grandparents and other relatives can add money to a Trump Account, even if they aren't the ones managing it. Contributions can add up over time, especially when multiple family members chip in. To get started, ask the account manager to send you a contribution link through the official Trump Accounts app or website. 
 Just remember that everyone shares the same $5,000 annual contribution limit, and the money is largely off limits until the child turns 18. 
 Can grandparents contribute to a Trump Account? FAQs 
 Do I need the parents' permission to contribute? 
 No formal parental permission is required to add money to the account, but you'll need a link from the account manager to start contributing.  
 What happens if total contributions go over $5,000? 
 The platform declines deposits above the cap and pauses recurring gifts until the next calendar year.  
 Can grandparents take a tax deduction for contributing? 
 Unlike some IRA contributions, your Trump Account gift isn't federally tax-deductible.
